nodes.label: Runtime Actors
nodes.summary: Human, agent, tool, and automation actors that operate inside the EG-Desk world.
nodes.body:
# Runtime Actors

Runtime actors are entities that can observe, decide, or act inside EG-Desk.

Examples:

- human user
- Codex root thread
- subagent
- browser controller
- terminal process
- MCP tool
- heartbeat automation
- external service

Actors should be described by coordinates, not just names:

```text
Actor = {
  reality_scope,
  architecture_scope,
  present_surface,
  past_sources,
  future_objective,
  multiverse_branch,
  allowed_actions,
  output_contract
}
```

This is where swarm design fits. A swarm is a coordinated pattern of runtime actors over the EG-Desk ontology, not the ontology's foundation.

nodes.label: Architecture Runtime
nodes.summary: Hardware and software topology that makes the EG-Desk world executable.
nodes.body:
# Architecture Runtime

Architecture runtime is the handle for the executable hardware/software environment EG-Desk is attached to.

It can include many objects:

- hardware: CPU, RAM, disk, GPU, sensors, power state
- OS and desktop: windows, files, apps, permissions, input devices
- execution surfaces: browser, terminal, editor, local app, cloud API, backend, DB
- code surfaces: repo, branch, worktree, test runner, build system
- EG-Desk surfaces: [[egdesk-desk.md]], [[egdesk-agenda.md]], [[egdesk-card.md]], [[egdesk-run-bubble.md]], [[egdesk-run-playback.md]]

Which of those objects are grouped together is a relation-map decision, not a universal definition of architecture.

## Existing Runtime Anchor

The current Firefox direction treats:

```text
egdesk.desk    = computer-level live work surface
egdesk.agenda  = work + execution environment pairing
egdesk.card    = view/runtime surface on the Desk
```

This ontology treats those as projections of architecture into the present work surface.

nodes.label: Space Axis
nodes.summary: Physical, spatial, and compute-object axis for real objects, hardware, files, surfaces, cards, and runtime resources.
nodes.body:
# Space Axis

The space axis is for physical, spatial, and compute-object reality.

It includes:

- people, companies, places, and devices
- CPU, RAM, disk, GPU, OS, browser, terminal, backend, database
- files, folders, repos, Drive documents, source refs as addressable objects
- visible panes, cards, canvas placement, and screen surfaces

## Rule

Space is not just visual layout. It is the object/surface/resource axis.

```text
Space
  -> physical object
  -> compute object
  -> file/storage object
  -> visible surface
```

Storage and topology are not separate primary axes. They are binding patterns inside or across Space, Time, and Virtual.

nodes.label: Time Axis
nodes.summary: Temporal axis for past evidence, present executable state, future goals, and alternate branches.
nodes.body:
# Time Axis

The time axis is for temporal state and transition.

In product-facing views, the main time axis flows left to right:

```text
Past -> Present -> Future
```

Backward references can exist as evidence lookup or memory retrieval, but the visible time axis should not be drawn as a bidirectional arrow unless the view is explicitly about branching, rewind, or comparison.

It includes:

- past evidence, memory, chat history, logs, revisions
- present executable state and active context
- future vision, goals, plans, tasks, and commitments
- multiverse branches, simulations, and hypothetical states
- events and actions as transitions

## Rule

Action is not a separate primary axis. It is a temporal transition that touches Space and Virtual.

```text
Action
  = Time transition
  + Space target
  + Virtual meaning
```

nodes.label: Virtual Axis
nodes.summary: Conceptual and semantic axis for entities, concepts, identities, intentions, goals, and meanings.
nodes.body:
# Virtual Axis

The virtual axis is for conceptual and semantic identity.

It includes:

- canonical concepts and entities
- ontology concepts
- goals, plans, tasks, blockers, decisions
- agent identity, role, memory, and context meaning
- source reference meaning, not just the bytes or path

## Rule

Intent is not a separate primary axis. It is a virtual meaning that becomes temporal commitment and spatial work.

```text
Intent
  = Virtual objective
  + Time commitment
  + Space artifact or action surface
```

nodes.label: Agenda
nodes.summary: EG-Desk work boundary pairing a task or objective with the execution environment needed to do it.
nodes.body:
# Agenda

Agenda is an EG-Desk product concept, not a generic todo list or folder.

An Agenda is the work boundary that pairs a task, objective, or project slice with the execution environment needed to do it.

An Agenda can include:

- browser cards
- file cards
- chat cards
- terminal cards
- agent/context bindings
- account/profile bindings
- result cards
- run bubbles and run playback

Agenda nesting is a work decomposition graph, not a folder tree. Deep structure can exist in data, while the Desk UI shows the active slice.

## Stable Definition

```text
Agenda = work + execution environment pairing
```

nodes.label: Card
nodes.summary: EG-Desk visible work/runtime surface on the Desk, optionally attached to a live runtime or source reference.
nodes.body:
# Card

Card is an EG-Desk product concept, not a generic rectangular UI element.

A Card is a visible work surface on the Desk. Some cards also own or attach to a runtime process, browser context, file view, chat session, terminal session, or generated artifact.

Card state is stored in Desk/world coordinates, not viewport pixels.

## Stable Definition

```text
Card = view/runtime surface on the Desk
```

The card concept covers a family of specific card types, such as browser card, file card, chat card, terminal card, result card, and ontology map card.

nodes.label: Desk
nodes.summary: EG-Desk's computer-level live work surface that projects OS, browser, file, process, account, and agent resources into one canvas.
nodes.body:
# Desk

Desk is an EG-Desk product concept, not a generic desktop definition.

In EG-Desk, a Desk is the computer-level live work surface. It should feel like using "my computer as a desk", while internally projecting OS, browser, process, file, account, and agent resources into a canvas.

Desk is not the same as:

- a browser profile
- a project folder
- a static canvas document
- the generic `desktop` object handle

The generic `desktop` handle can represent the visible operating plane. `egdesk.desk` is the product-level concept that gives that plane EG-Desk behavior, state, source refs, agenda membership, and runtime attachment rules.

## Stable Definition

```text
Desk = computer-level live work surface
```

Desk contains Agendas and Cards. Its concrete runtime grouping may still be declared by relation maps.

nodes.label: Canvas-Native Ontology Rendering Plan
nodes.summary: Plan for rendering EG-Desk ontology directly on the EG-Desk infinite canvas.
nodes.body:
# Canvas-Native Ontology Rendering Plan

The ontology should not become a standalone marketing website as its final home.

The source of truth is Markdown. The primary viewing surface is EG-Desk's infinite canvas. A separate browser page may exist as a development harness later, but the product-facing concept should render as an EG-Desk canvas card or canvas-native view.

The highest-value Markdown units are relation maps, not encyclopedia-like object definitions. Object pages can stay thin; relation maps declare the custom hierarchy and assembly that matter for the current work.

## Direction

```text
ontology/*.md
  -> parser
  -> graph.json
  -> EG-Desk Ontology Map Card
      -> canonical concept selection
      -> three-axis focus view
      -> identity rail
      -> node detail
      -> context bundle
```

## Product Placement

There are two product placements for the same renderer:

1. `Ontology Map Card`
   - interactive work surface inside EG-Desk
   - supports coordinate-lens navigation, local pan/zoom, object selection, relation selection, and context loading
   - does not expose hierarchy/time/spatial/focus/tilt as user-facing mode buttons

2. `About / Vision curated preset`
   - read-only or guided view using the same graph data
   - explains EG-Desk's world model to a user without turning the first screen into a landing page

## Primary Focus Layout

The product-facing focus layout should use time-sliced spatial panes.

```text
Past Pane  ->    Present Pane(active)  ->    Future Pane
space@past       space@present               space@future
```

The concrete visualization method is [[views/time-sliced-flat-deck.md]].

Rules:

- Time arranges panes horizontally in one direction: past on the left, present in the center, future on the right.
- A physical pane is a real surface/container object.
- Each time slice has a time-local virtual pane assembled from the physical pane and its evidence/meaning.
- A trajectory pane is the assembled semantic/time-space across past, present, and future.
- Objects live on physical panes: cards, files, runtime resources, surfaces, and people.
- Virtual concepts are overlays or identity bindings attached to objects on physical panes, time-local virtual panes, and the trajectory pane.
- `storage`, `topology`, `intent`, and `action` are binding types inside or between panes, not primary axes.
- The product view should wrap all relevant levels: physical pane wrappers around actual panes, time-local virtual pane wrappers inside each slice, and a trajectory pane wrapper around the composed time-sliced space.
- Pane labels should be unnecessary in the product view; the time-flow position, active emphasis, wrappers, and contained objects should make each pane's role inferable.
- Internal strata such as object layer, binding band, axis, and virtual overlay should be visualized with bands, ribbons, anchors, and containment rather than written as labels in the canvas.
- Focus mode should avoid global graph edges. It should show selected-object projections and selected-only relation details.
- The current visualization method is a flat 2D deck seen from a shallow 2.5D camera angle. Pane thickness is not semantic; the angle only makes adjacent time panes and depth layers readable together.

## Projection Types

The renderer may keep hierarchy, time, and spatial projections as internal development presets over the same canonical concept model, but the product interaction should not ask the user to choose these as modes.

```text
canonical concept
  + facet
  + view rule
  = projection node
```

### Hierarchy

Answers:

```text
Where does this concept belong?
What contains what?
What should the LLM load first?
```

### Time

Answers:

```text
How does evidence become present state?
How does present action update future plans?
Where do branches and simulations live?
```

### Spatial

Answers:

```text
Where is this concept placed in the EG-Desk world?
Which runtime surface, actor, sourceRef, and objective are connected?
```

Spatial starts as a 2D pane layout:

```text
2D pane layout
+ layer/depth emphasis
+ connection lines
+ layer clusters
```

2.5D or full 3D can come later only if thickness has a clear semantic role. The default pane should remain flat.

### Time-Sliced Pane Focus

Answers:

```text
Which time pane is active?
Which objects live on that space-at-time pane?
Which virtual identity overlays those objects?
Which binding types are active in this pane?
```

This is the mode needed for concepts such as `entity.llm_chat_session`, where the active present pane contains spatial objects such as a chat card/session file/runtime, while virtual identity and intent overlay those objects and the side panes show past/future context.

### Pane Inventory

Pane inventory answers:

```text
What objects are present in this time-local pane?
Which physical, storage, topology, intent, and action objects should be scanned together?
Which object should become the next object focus?
```

Interaction rule:

- click pane empty space -> pane inventory
- click an inventory object -> object focus
- click a layer band -> emphasize that layer in the selected time pane
- horizontal trackpad scroll -> move across time panes
- vertical trackpad scroll -> emphasize one visual stratum in the selected time pane
- pinch or Cmd/Ctrl + wheel -> semantic zoom
- blank-pane drag -> card-local pan
- click relation stroke -> side-panel relation detail
- show a bounded inventory cluster, not all global graph edges
- avoid generic mode toolbar controls such as focus/hierarchy/time/spatial or virtual/physical buttons

Visual rule:

- use unlabeled depth bands for physical / binding / virtual
- show connection points on inventory objects
- show orthogonal tree connectors for assembly/containment, such as desktop -> terminal -> cpu/ram/disk
- show actual node-to-node connectors for co-present graph edges; depth connectors are structure, not semantic relation evidence
- avoid visible relation label chips in the canvas; keep the visual reading simple

## MVP

The first implementation should be deliberately small:

- Parse Markdown frontmatter and wiki links into `graph.json`.
- Copy `graph.json` into Firefox chrome resources.
- Add a Dock entry that opens an `Ontology Map` card.
- Render nodes and edges in SVG.
- Support card-local pan and zoom.
- Render one coordinate-lens view first.
- Keep projection presets internal until there is a product reason to expose them.
- Show selected node detail from parsed Markdown summary/body.

## Next Renderer Step

The next renderer step should not add more global edge density. It should add selection-driven three-axis focus:

- selected canonical concept
- active time pane
- identity rail for sibling projections
- binding chips for storage/topology/intent/action
- side pane previews for past/future context

## Non-Goals For MVP

- No full Markdown editor.
- No graph mutation UI.
- No external web app requirement.
- No real Three.js scene yet.
- No attempt to replace the existing Desk/Agenda/Card runtime model.

nodes.label: EG-Desk Ontology
nodes.summary: Entry point for the EG-Desk ontology source of truth.
nodes.body:
# EG-Desk Ontology

This folder is the source-of-truth seed for EG-Desk's ontology-aware operating world.

The ontology should be readable as Markdown, linkable like Obsidian, and parseable by a local web UI. The web UI can render graphs, timelines, and detail panels, but it should not become the source of truth.

## Core Sentence

EG-Desk is an ontology-aware operating desk that projects reality, compute architecture, and time-axis representatives into a live work surface.

```text
Reality
+ Hardware and software architecture
+ Time-axis representatives
  - Past
  - Present
  - Future
  - Multiverse
= EG-Desk virtual operating world
```

## Primary Load Order

For an LLM or parser, start here:

1. [[concepts/egdesk-world.md]]
2. [[schema.md]]
3. [[concepts/canonical-concept.md]]
4. [[concepts/facet.md]]
5. [[concepts/axes/axis-space.md]]
6. [[concepts/axes/axis-time.md]]
7. [[concepts/axes/axis-virtual.md]]
8. [[concepts/binding-type.md]]
9. [[concepts/projection.md]]
10. [[concepts/cross-facet-binding.md]]
11. [[concepts/view-projection.md]]
12. [[concepts/identity-rail.md]]
13. [[concepts/time-sliced-spatial-pane.md]]
14. [[views/time-sliced-flat-deck.md]]
15. [[concepts/facets/facet-space.md]]
16. [[concepts/facets/facet-topology.md]]
17. [[concepts/facets/facet-time.md]]
18. [[concepts/facets/facet-storage.md]]
19. [[concepts/facets/facet-intent.md]]
20. [[concepts/facets/facet-action.md]]
21. [[concepts/reality.md]]
22. [[concepts/architecture-runtime.md]]
23. [[concepts/time-past.md]]
24. [[concepts/time-present.md]]
25. [[concepts/time-future.md]]
26. [[concepts/time-multiverse.md]]
27. [[concepts/operation-layer.md]]
28. [[concepts/actor-runtime.md]]
29. [[concepts/source-ref.md]]
30. [[concepts/structured-output.md]]
31. [[concepts/egdesk-desk.md]]
32. [[concepts/egdesk-agenda.md]]
33. [[concepts/egdesk-card.md]]
34. [[concepts/egdesk-run-bubble.md]]
35. [[concepts/egdesk-run-playback.md]]

For concrete assembly examples, load:

1. [[examples/llm-chat-session.md]]
2. [[examples/desktop-runtime.md]]
3. [[examples/chat-memory.md]]

For custom relation maps, load:

1. [[maps/local-runtime-inventory.md]]
2. [[maps/llm-chat-runtime-assembly.md]]

For visual overviews, open:

1. [[views/egdesk-world-graph.md]]
2. [[views/faceted-concept-model.md]]
3. [[views/time-sliced-flat-deck.md]]

For the canvas-native rendering path, open [[canvas-rendering-plan.md]].

## Boundary

Subagents, tools, browser controllers, and human collaborators are runtime actors inside the EG-Desk world. They are not the root ontology.

The root ontology is:

```text
canonical concepts
  -> three primary axes
      -> Space
      -> Time
      -> Virtual
  -> binding types
      -> storage / topology / intent / action
  -> world topology
      -> reality
      -> architecture
      -> time representatives
      -> operation layer
      -> actors and actions
```

Hierarchy is axis-local. A physical pane is a real surface/container object; each time slice also has a time-local virtual pane assembled from physical evidence and meaning. Past, present, and future are then wrapped again by a trajectory pane. Objects live on physical panes, and virtual concepts act as semantic overlays or identity bindings on those objects and across the composed virtual panes. Storage, topology, intent, and action describe how Space, Time, and Virtual intertwine.

## Concept Definition Boundary

Use different document weights for different concept classes:

```text
generic object handles
  -> thin page
  -> aliases / abbreviations / source identity hints
  -> relation maps declare context-specific assembly

EG-Desk product concepts
  -> short real definition
  -> boundaries against generic meanings
  -> stable product relations
  -> relation maps only for specific runtime assembly
```

Examples:

- `desktop` is a generic object handle for the visible operating plane.
- `egdesk.desk` is the EG-Desk product concept for a computer-level live work surface.
- `terminal`, `cpu`, `ram`, and `disk` stay thin handles.
- `egdesk.agenda`, `egdesk.card`, `egdesk.run_bubble`, and `egdesk.run_playback` keep product definitions because their meaning is custom to EG-Desk.

## Existing Project Anchors

This ontology wraps existing EG-Desk product/runtime decisions rather than replacing them:

- `Desk / Agenda / Card`: `apps/firefox-ui-demo/docs/DESK_AGENDA_CARD_RUNTIME_MODEL.md`
- `Chat / Canvas / Agent layer`: `apps/firefox-ui-demo/docs/CHAT_CANVAS_AGENT_LAYER_MODEL.md`
- `Run Playback`: `apps/firefox-ui-demo/docs/CANVAS_RUN_PLAYBACK_MODEL.md`
- `Browser Agent Observation`: `apps/firefox-ui-demo/docs/BROWSER_AGENT_OBSERVATION_RUNTIME.md`
- `Ontology Bridge`: `docs/vision/ontology-bridge.md`

nodes.label: Ontology Schema
nodes.summary: Minimal Markdown/frontmatter schema for EG-Desk ontology concepts.
nodes.body:
# Ontology Schema

Each ontology file is a graph node. Markdown body is for human reading. Frontmatter is for parsers and LLM context selection.

The ontology is not meant to become a Wikipedia clone. Basic object pages such as `terminal`, `cpu`, or `disk` can be thin handles. EG-Desk product concepts such as `egdesk.desk`, `egdesk.agenda`, or `egdesk.card` should keep short definitions because their meaning is custom to EG-Desk. The most important authored units for context-specific hierarchy are relation maps: notes that declare how objects are assembled for a specific work context.

## Required Frontmatter

```yaml
id: time.present
type: representative
layer: time
summary: Current executable state of the EG-Desk world.
relations:
  receives_from:
    - time.past
  drives:
    - action.execution
```

## Stable Fields

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `id` | Stable machine id. Prefer dotted ids. |
| `type` | Concept category such as `world`, `representative`, `surface`, `actor`, `primitive`. |
| `layer` | Coarse grouping such as `reality`, `architecture`, `time`, `operation`, `runtime`, `evidence`. |
| `summary` | One-line context summary for LLM preloading and graph labels. |
| `aliases` | Thin object-name variants, alternate spellings, or common labels. |
| `abbreviations` | Ambiguous short forms mapped to possible expansions. |
| `relations` | Typed edges to other concept ids. |
| `relation_edges` | Edges declared by a relation map between arbitrary source and target ids. |

## Object Handle Metadata

Object pages should stay thin, but they can carry name-disambiguation metadata.

```yaml
id: moq
type: object_handle
layer: operation
summary: Object handle for an ambiguous MOQ token in a specific work context.
aliases:
  - MOQ
  - M.O.Q.
abbreviations:
  MOQ:
    - minimum order quantity
    - message-oriented queue
```

This does not define a universal concept. It only tells the parser and LLM what names may point at the same handle, and what ambiguity should be preserved.

## Product Concept Definitions

EG-Desk-specific concepts should have definitions because they are not generic world objects.

```yaml
id: egdesk.card
type: product_concept
layer: runtime
summary: EG-Desk visible work/runtime surface on the Desk.
aliases:
  - Card
relations:
  operates_inside:
    - egdesk.desk
  binds:
    - source.ref
```

Keep these definitions short. They should explain the EG-Desk meaning, the boundary against generic meanings, and stable product relations. Do not put every possible runtime composition into the product concept page; use relation maps for that.

## Relation Map Notes

Use relation map notes when the value is in the user's custom assembly, not in the generic definition of a concept.

```yaml
id: map.llm_chat_runtime_assembly
type: relation_map
layer: architecture
summary: Custom runtime assembly for understanding an LLM chat session inside EG-Desk.
relations:
  organizes:
    - entity.llm_chat_session
relation_edges:
  - source: desktop
    relation: contains
    target: terminal
  - source: terminal
    relation: uses
    target: cpu
```

This means:

```text
terminal.md says what object handle "terminal" refers to.
map.llm_chat_runtime_assembly.md says how terminal is assembled in this context.
```

The same object can participate in a different relation map for another domain.

## Faceted Modeling Fields

These can appear in frontmatter for simple cases or in the Markdown body for richer examples. The current parser treats frontmatter as the graph edge source and Markdown as human/LLM context.

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `canonical_id` | Stable identity shared by projections of the same thing. |
| `facet` | Lens used by a projection, such as `facet.space` or `facet.time`. |
| `projection_id` | Stable id for a drawable projection node. |
| `view` | Intended view preset or rendering mode. |
| `source_ref` | Durable pointer to the file, repo, DB row, URL, or runtime state backing the concept. |
| `axis` | Primary axis for a projection: `axis.space`, `axis.time`, or `axis.virtual`. |
| `binding_type` | Intertwining pattern such as `storage`, `topology`, `intent`, or `action`. |

Projection ids should make the facet obvious:

```text
projection.<canonical>.<facet>.<local_name>
```

Example:

```text
projection.llm_chat_session.storage.session_file
```

## Relation Vocabulary

Start with a small relation set:

| Relation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `contains` | Parent concept contains child concepts inside the same axis or runtime stratum. |
| `part_of` | Child concept belongs to a same-stratum parent assembly. |
| `implemented_by` | Virtual/product object is realized through information and physical objects. |
| `runs_on` | Information/runtime object executes on a physical substrate. |
| `stored_in` | Information object or evidence is persisted in a storage substrate. |
| `represents` | Node represents a real, information, or virtual thing. |
| `projects_into` | Source is projected into a runtime/view layer. |
| `receives_from` | Node is updated by another node. |
| `drives` | Node drives another node or action. |
| `acts_on` | Actor/action acts on a target surface/object. |
| `observes` | Node observes target state without owning it. |
| `records` | Node records traces/evidence about target. |
| `branches_into` | Node can produce alternate branches or futures. |
| `branches_from` | Node branches from a current state, goal, or plan. |
| `binds` | Node binds a concept to a runtime resource. |
| `derived_from` | Node is derived from another node or evidence. |
| `represented_by` | Abstract concept is represented by concrete runtime/evidence nodes. |
| `provides_evidence_for` | Evidence-bearing node supports another node. |
| `updates` | Node mutates or refreshes another node. |
| `uses` | Node depends on a primitive, actor, or resource. |
| `informs` | Node influences another node without directly updating it. |
| `operates_inside` | Actor/process is scoped inside a world or surface. |
| `receives_constraints_from` | Node is governed by another node's constraints. |
| `constrains` | Node limits or governs another node. |
| `visualizes` | View node visualizes another concept or graph. |
| `visualized_by` | Concept is visualized by a view node. |
| `implements` | Plan or artifact implements a concept or decision. |
| `same_identity_as` | Projection shares canonical identity with another projection. |
| `projects_as` | Canonical concept projects into a specific projection node. |

## Faceted Modeling Rule

Do not use one hierarchy to represent every axis.

```text
Canonical Concept
  -> Space axis projection
  -> Time axis projection
  -> Virtual axis projection
  -> Binding types between axes
```

The primary axes are:

```text
Space
Time
Virtual
```

`storage`, `topology`, `intent`, and `action` are binding types, not primary axes.

Containment is valid only inside one primary axis.

Cross-facet relations should be explicit bindings, identity-rail entries, or selected-focus connectors.

## Context Loading Rule

An LLM should not load the whole ontology by default.

```text
index.md
  -> selected concept files
  -> selected relation neighbors
  -> source docs only when needed
```

## Web UI Rule

The web UI may cache parsed nodes and edges, but generated caches are secondary. The canonical source remains Markdown frontmatter and links.

The renderer should draw projections as the primary screen nodes and preserve canonical identity in the detail panel or identity rail.

nodes.label: Run Bubble
nodes.summary: Inspectable EG-Desk record of the plan, action, context, evidence, and provenance for one AI or automation run.
nodes.body:
# Run Bubble

Run Bubble is an EG-Desk product concept.

It is the inspectable record for one run: plan, action, context, evidence, intermediate artifacts, and provenance. It is not hidden model reasoning. It is the user-facing, checkable trace EG-Desk can preserve.

## Stable Definition

```text
Run Bubble = inspectable plan/action/context record for one run
```

nodes.label: Run Playback
nodes.summary: Canvas-native guided playback that lets the user inspect how a result was derived across cards, evidence, and steps.
nodes.body:
# Run Playback

Run Playback is an EG-Desk product concept.

It is the guided, step-by-step canvas walkthrough for a result. It lets the user follow derivation spatially on the Desk: what evidence was used, which cards mattered, what changed, and how the final output emerged.

Run Playback is related to Run Bubble, but they are not the same:

- Run Bubble stores the inspectable record.
- Run Playback presents a guided temporal/spatial walkthrough.

## Stable Definition

```text
Run Playback = guided canvas replay for one run
```

nodes.label: EG-Desk World
nodes.summary: The virtual operating world formed by reality, architecture, and time representatives.
nodes.body:
# EG-Desk World

EG-Desk is not primarily a chat UI, a task runner, or a swarm manager.

It is a virtual operating world layered over reality and compute architecture. It lets the user see and manipulate work through time-aware representatives:

- [[reality.md]]: real companies, people, machines, files, services, customers, and accounts.
- [[architecture-runtime.md]]: hardware, OS, browser, terminal, app, cloud, repo, and database surfaces.
- [[time-past.md]]: evidence, logs, prior messages, git history, file revisions, and execution traces.
- [[time-present.md]]: current executable state and active work surface.
- [[time-future.md]]: vision, goals, plans, and tasks.
- [[time-multiverse.md]]: alternate branches, simulations, hypothetical states, and candidate futures.

Runtime actors such as humans, Codex, subagents, tools, browser controllers, and automation jobs operate inside this world. They should be assigned coordinates in the ontology rather than treated as the ontology itself.

## Design Implication

Swarm design comes after world design.

```text
EG-Desk World
  -> defines surfaces, evidence, time, permissions, and source refs
Runtime Actors
  -> operate inside those definitions
Swarm
  -> coordinated actor pattern, not the root model
```

The world is also faceted. One drawn hierarchy is not enough.

```text
Canonical Concept
  -> Space projection
  -> Topology projection
  -> Time projection
  -> Storage projection
  -> Intent projection
  -> Action projection
```

Hierarchy, overlap, and containment are lens-local. Cross-lens truth is represented by [[cross-facet-binding.md]] and surfaced through [[identity-rail.md]].

nodes.label: Chat Memory
nodes.summary: Canonical identity for chat memory as temporal evidence, stored trace, context input, and read action.
nodes.body:
# Chat Memory

Chat memory is a useful stress test because it can be understood as an object or a verb.

As an object, it may be a stored trace.

As a temporal representative, it is Past evidence.

As a runtime operation, it is read, summarized, selected, or ignored.

## Facet Projections

| Facet | Projection | Valid Reading |
|---|---|---|
| Time | `projection.chat_memory.time.past_evidence` | Prior messages, tool calls, and decisions are Past evidence. |
| Storage | `projection.chat_memory.storage.trace_file` | The memory has a durable source reference such as a log, file, index, or database row. |
| Intent | `projection.chat_memory.intent.context_input` | The memory is selected because it helps the current objective. |
| Action | `projection.chat_memory.action.file_read` | Loading memory is a verb: read, retrieve, summarize, and bind to present context. |

## Modeling Rule

Do not force chat memory into only one of these:

```text
file object
past state
context source
read action
```

It is a canonical concept with facet projections.

nodes.label: Desktop Runtime
nodes.summary: Canonical identity for the local desktop runtime across visible space, system topology, storage, and actions.
nodes.body:
# Desktop Runtime

Desktop runtime is both a visible workspace and an execution substrate.

Those are not the same projection.

## Facet Projections

| Facet | Projection | Valid Reading |
|---|---|---|
| Space | `projection.desktop_runtime.space.desktop_plane` | The visible desktop/canvas plane that contains cards and panes. |
| Topology | `projection.desktop_runtime.topology.hardware_os` | The Mac/Windows/Linux runtime composed of CPU, RAM, Disk, GPU, OS, browser, terminal, helper services, and network. |
| Storage | `projection.desktop_runtime.storage.local_disk` | Local filesystem and app state that can persist sessions, source files, logs, and caches. |
| Action | `projection.desktop_runtime.action.app_execution` | App execution, shell commands, browser operations, file IO, and automation steps. |

## Relation Map Rule

The chat card can be visibly inside the desktop plane while the chat runtime uses topology resources and writes storage traces. Those statements should be authored in relation maps, not as universal definitions of desktop, terminal, disk, CPU, or RAM.

```text
Space:
  Desktop plane contains Chat Card

Topology:
  Chat Runtime depends on Desktop Runtime

Storage:
  Chat Session File is stored on Disk
```

These are three different statements. The renderer must keep their facet labels visible or inferable.

For the current EG-Desk LLM chat context, see `map.llm_chat_runtime_assembly`.

nodes.label: LLM Chat Session
nodes.summary: Canonical identity for an LLM chat session across space, topology, storage, time, intent, and action facets.
nodes.body:
# LLM Chat Session

This example is the canonical test case for faceted ontology rendering.

An LLM chat session cannot be honestly represented by one hierarchy.

It is primarily a Virtual entity that is anchored into Space and Time.

## Primary Axis Projections

| Axis | Projection | Valid Reading |
|---|---|---|
| Virtual | `entity.llm_chat_session` | The canonical semantic identity of the chat session. |
| Space | `projection.llm_chat_session.space.chat_card` | The chat appears as a card or panel on the Desk. |
| Time | `projection.llm_chat_session.time.memory_trace` | Prior messages and tool calls become Past evidence used by the present turn. |

## Binding Types

| Binding | Projection | Axis Intertwine |
|---|---|---|
| Topology | `projection.llm_chat_session.topology.runtime` | Space compute resources + Virtual runtime identity + Present executable state. |
| Storage | `projection.llm_chat_session.storage.session_file` | Space file object + Virtual source identity + Time history/revision. |
| Intent | `projection.llm_chat_session.intent.context_binding` | Virtual objective + Time commitment + Space artifact/action surface. |
| Action | `projection.llm_chat_session.action.message_send` | Time transition + Space target + Virtual operation meaning. |

## Binding Rule

The projections are connected by identity and relation maps, not by forced containment.

```text
entity.llm_chat_session
  has projections in multiple facets
  binds to entity.chat_memory
  binds to entity.desktop_runtime
```

The concrete runtime assembly for this example belongs in `map.llm_chat_runtime_assembly`.

## Rendering Rule

Default view:

```text
Show one active facet projection.
```

On selection:

```text
Show identity rail:
  Virtual -> LLM Chat Session
  Space   -> Chat Card / Runtime / Session File anchors
  Time    -> Memory Trace / Message Events
  Binding -> topology / storage / intent / action
```

Do not draw every relation all the time. Reveal cross-facet bindings only when the selected concept needs them.

nodes.label: Action Facet
nodes.summary: Lens for verbs, events, operations, side effects, and executable transitions.
nodes.body:
# Action Facet

The action facet describes what happens.

It is the facet for:

- read
- write
- click
- type
- message send
- tool call
- file edit
- command execution
- deployment
- state transition

## Containment Rule

Action containment means sequence, transaction, or suboperation.

```text
Implement feature
  contains read files
  contains edit files
  contains run verification
  contains report result
```

An action projection may touch storage, topology, time, and space, but it should remain a verb/event rather than being flattened into an object hierarchy.

## Example

For `entity.llm_chat_session`, action projections may be:

```text
projection.llm_chat_session.action.message_send
projection.llm_chat_session.action.file_read
projection.llm_chat_session.action.context_assemble
projection.llm_chat_session.action.tool_call
```

nodes.label: Intent Facet
nodes.summary: Lens for purpose, objective, goal, plan, task, and decision pressure.
nodes.body:
# Intent Facet

The intent facet describes why a concept matters in the work system.

It is the facet for:

- user objective
- goal
- plan
- task
- decision blocker
- acceptance condition
- priority and scope

## Containment Rule

Intent containment means objective decomposition.

```text
Vision
  contains goal
  contains plan
  contains task
```

This does not mean the task is physically stored inside the future or visually contained inside the card.

## Example

For `entity.llm_chat_session`, the intent projection may be:

```text
projection.llm_chat_session.intent.context_binding
  label: Active Context Binding
  objective: answer or execute the user's current request
  acceptance: the requested work is complete and verified
```

nodes.label: Space Facet
nodes.summary: Lens for visible spatial placement, overlap, panes, cards, and canvas geography.
nodes.body:
# Space Facet

The space facet describes where a concept appears in the visible EG-Desk canvas.

It is the facet for:

- desktop panes
- cards
- panels
- 2D/2.5D canvas placement
- visible overlap
- camera position, pan, zoom, and tilt

## Containment Rule

Spatial containment means visible containment only.

```text
Desktop pane
  contains Browser Card
  contains Chat Card
  contains Ontology Map Card
```

It does not automatically mean runtime ownership, file storage, memory, or intent ownership.

## Example

For `entity.llm_chat_session`, the space projection may be:

```text
projection.llm_chat_session.space.chat_card
  label: Chat Card
  parent plane: Desktop
  readable as: the user-facing place where the conversation is visible
```

nodes.label: Storage Facet
nodes.summary: Lens for durable storage identity, file paths, repos, databases, and source references.
nodes.body:
# Storage Facet

The storage facet describes where durable bytes and references live.

It is the facet for:

- local files
- session logs
- Git repos
- databases
- Drive documents
- caches
- source references

## Containment Rule

Storage containment means resource address containment.

```text
Disk
  contains folder
  contains file

Repo
  contains tracked source file

Database
  contains table
  contains row
```

A storage node can represent the same canonical concept as a space or time node, but it should not be merged into those hierarchies.

## Example

For `entity.llm_chat_session`, the storage projection may be:

```text
projection.llm_chat_session.storage.session_file
  label: Session File
  address: local session log or database row
  source_ref: stable pointer used for reload
```

nodes.label: Time Facet
nodes.summary: Lens for past evidence, present executable state, future plans, and multiverse branches.
nodes.body:
# Time Facet

The time facet describes when a concept exists or acts.

It is the facet for:

- past evidence and memory
- present executable state
- future goals, plans, and tasks
- multiverse branches and simulations
- causal order

## Containment Rule

Time containment means temporal membership or causality.

```text
Past
  contains chat history
  contains file revision
  contains execution log

Future
  contains goal
  contains plan
  contains task
```

This does not mean the past memory is visually inside a desktop card or physically inside the CPU.

## Example

For `entity.llm_chat_session`, the time projection may be:

```text
projection.llm_chat_session.time.memory_trace
  label: Chat Memory Trace
  phase: Past
  evidence: messages, tool calls, decisions, summaries
```

nodes.label: Topology Facet
nodes.summary: Lens for runtime dependency, resource use, system architecture, and execution topology.
nodes.body:
# Topology Facet

The topology facet describes how runtime objects depend on each other.

It is the facet for:

- hardware and OS resources
- app, browser, terminal, helper, API, backend, and database paths
- resource dependency
- execution boundary
- local versus cloud placement

## Containment Rule

Topology containment means runtime composition or dependency, not visual overlap.

```text
Desktop runtime
  uses OS
  uses CPU
  uses RAM
  uses Disk

LLM chat session
  uses model runtime
  uses context window
  uses tool bridge
```

The topology facet can show that a chat session uses CPU/RAM while the space facet shows that the same session is a card on the desktop.

## Example

For `entity.llm_chat_session`, the topology projection may be:

```text
projection.llm_chat_session.topology.runtime
  label: Chat Runtime
  reads from: context window
  calls: tool bridge
  depends on: CPU/RAM/network/model endpoint
```

nodes.label: Binding Type
nodes.summary: Intertwining pattern between Space, Time, and Virtual axes.
nodes.body:
# Binding Type

Binding types explain how the three primary axes intertwine.

They are not primary axes.

## Core Binding Types

```text
storage
  = Space address/object
  + Virtual identity/source meaning
  + Time revision/history/snapshot

topology
  = Space compute resources
  + Virtual dependency/runtime identity
  + Time current executable state

intent
  = Virtual objective
  + Time commitment
  + Space artifact/surface

action
  = Time transition
  + Space target
  + Virtual operation meaning
```

The renderer should show binding types as strips, chips, or intersection bands between axes rather than as top-level panes.

nodes.label: Canonical Concept
nodes.summary: Stable identity for a thing before it is projected into a specific lens or view.
nodes.body:
# Canonical Concept

A canonical concept is the stable identity of a thing in the EG-Desk world.

It is not the same as the node drawn on screen. A screen node is a [[projection.md]] of a canonical concept through a specific [[facet.md]].

## Rule

```text
Canonical Concept
  !=
View Node
```

The same canonical concept can appear differently depending on lens:

```text
entity.llm_chat_session
  space projection    -> Chat Card on Desk
  topology projection -> runtime session using CPU/RAM
  storage projection  -> session JSONL on Disk
  time projection     -> Past memory trace
  intent projection   -> active context/goal binding
  action projection   -> message-send / file-read / context-assemble
```

This prevents EG-Desk from forcing multi-facet things into a single false hierarchy.

## Visual Rule

When a user selects a concept, the renderer should keep canonical identity stable while allowing the active lens to change.

```text
Select canonical concept
  -> show active lens projection
  -> show identity rail with other facet projections
  -> show cross-facet bindings only for the selected concept
```

nodes.label: Cross-Facet Binding
nodes.summary: Connection between projections of the same canonical concept or between different facets.
nodes.body:
# Cross-Facet Binding

Cross-facet binding connects projections without pretending they belong in the same hierarchy.

Example:

```text
entity.llm_chat_session
  Space projection: Chat Card
  Storage projection: session JSONL file
  Time projection: Past memory trace
```

These projections are the same canonical concept from different lenses. They should be linked through identity binding, not by nesting all of them into one plane.

## Visual Rule

Show cross-facet bindings only when useful:

- selected concept identity rail
- hover/focus highlight
- explicit cross-lens mode

Do not show all cross-facet bindings by default.

nodes.label: Facet
nodes.summary: Secondary lens or binding view over the three primary axes.
nodes.body:
# Facet

A facet is a lens over the EG-Desk world.

Primary axes are not the same as facets.

```text
Primary axes:
  Space
  Time
  Virtual

Binding / secondary facets:
  storage
  topology
  intent
  action
```

Facets answer:

```text
Which aspect of this canonical concept are we looking at?
Which containment rules are valid in this view?
Which edges should be visible by default?
```

## Primary Axes

- [[axes/axis-space.md]]
- [[axes/axis-time.md]]
- [[axes/axis-virtual.md]]

## Secondary Facets / Binding Views

- [[facets/facet-space.md]]
- [[facets/facet-topology.md]]
- [[facets/facet-time.md]]
- [[facets/facet-storage.md]]
- [[facets/facet-intent.md]]
- [[facets/facet-action.md]]

## Containment Rule

Containment and visual overlap are valid only inside a single primary axis.

```text
Valid:
  Space axis: Desktop contains Browser Card
  Space axis: Disk contains session JSONL file
  Time axis: Past contains evidence trace
  Virtual axis: Goal contains tasks

Invalid:
  Desktop visually contains Past memory just because the memory is stored on disk.
```

Cross-axis relations should use [[binding-type.md]], [[cross-facet-binding.md]], ports, or identity rail entries instead of overlap.

nodes.label: Projection
nodes.summary: The representation of a canonical concept inside one facet.
nodes.body:
# Projection

A projection is how a canonical concept appears inside a specific facet.

Projection nodes are what the renderer draws.

```text
canonical concept + facet + view rules = projection node
```

## Projection Shape

```yaml
canonical_id: entity.llm_chat_session
facet: facet.storage
projection_id: projection.llm_chat_session.storage.file
shape: file
label: Session JSONL
source_ref: ~/.codex/sessions/...
```

## Renderer Rule

The renderer should draw projections, not raw canonical concepts.

The detail panel can show canonical identity and all available projections.

nodes.label: Operation Layer
nodes.summary: The LLM-aware layer that maps reality, architecture, and time representatives into action.
nodes.body:
# Operation Layer

The Operation Layer is where LLMs, tools, automation, and human decisions interact with the EG-Desk world.

It does four things:

1. Recognizes real-world objects and places behind digital resources.
2. Binds those objects to executable surfaces through source refs.
3. Performs actions through runtime actors and tools.
4. Emits structured outputs that update Past, Present, Future, or Multiverse.

The Operation Layer is not identical to a single model or subagent. It is the mapping and execution layer that lets many actor types work inside the same ontology.

nodes.label: Structured Output
nodes.summary: Machine-readable output that updates time representatives and can become context.
nodes.body:
# Structured Output

Structured Output is the bridge from action to reusable world state.

Examples:

- state diff
- decision record
- plan update
- task list
- evidence bundle
- artifact manifest
- source-ref list
- branch comparison
- run playback record

Structured Output should be both human-readable and machine-readable. It is how EG-Desk turns an action into future context without forcing the LLM to reread an entire transcript.

## Output Contract Shape

```yaml
id: output.example
type: decision_record
summary: One-line result.
updates:
  future:
    goals: []
    plans: []
  past:
    evidence_refs: []
  present:
    changed_surfaces: []
source_refs: []
```

nodes.label: Reality
nodes.summary: The external real world that EG-Desk represents, observes, and acts upon.
nodes.body:
# Reality

Reality is the external world EG-Desk is attached to.

Examples:

- people, companies, customers, departments
- physical computers and devices
- OS accounts and cloud accounts
- files, folders, repositories, databases
- browser sessions and authenticated websites
- business objects such as contracts, inquiries, reports, invoices, products

The ontology must not flatten these into file paths or chat messages only. EG-Desk should preserve the richer real-world categories and then bind them to digital resources through [[source-ref.md]].

## Relation To Existing Vision

The current EG-Desk Ontology Bridge frames this as a gap between physical objects/places and flattened digital objects/places. This concept keeps that direction, but expands it to include compute topology and time representatives.

Terminal is an object handle for command-line execution surfaces.

nodes.label: Future Representative
nodes.summary: Intent-bearing representative of desired states and planned work.
nodes.body:
# Future Representative

Future is the intent-bearing representative.

It includes:

- Vision: durable direction and product/business intent
- Goals: active objectives
- Plans: human-readable work structure
- Tasks: executable work units

Future answers:

```text
Where are we trying to go?
Why does the next action matter?
What sequence should turn possible state into real state?
```

Future should be connected to Present through executable tasks, not left as a static roadmap.

nodes.label: Multiverse Representative
nodes.summary: Representative of alternate branches, simulations, and candidate futures.
nodes.body:
# Multiverse Representative

Multiverse is the representative for possible worlds.

Examples:

- alternate implementation plans
- simulated user reactions
- possible UI states
- branch/worktree futures
- rollback paths
- product strategy options
- hypothetical company or customer states

Multiverse answers:

```text
What could happen?
What path should we choose?
What should remain only a simulation?
What branch can be tested without committing it to reality?
```

This layer is necessary because EG-Desk should support planning, simulation, and branching without confusing those possibilities with current reality.

nodes.label: Past Representative
nodes.summary: Evidence-bearing representative of prior states, actions, and artifacts.
nodes.body:
# Past Representative

Past is not just memory. It is the evidence-bearing representative of prior world states.

Examples:

- chat history
- tool history
- execution logs
- git history
- file revisions
- browser history
- screenshots and snapshots
- run playback records
- source references and provenance notes

Past answers:

```text
What happened?
What did we know?
What changed?
What can be replayed, cited, compared, or rolled back?
```

Past provides evidence to [[time-present.md]] and [[structured-output.md]]. It should be compactly indexable so an LLM can load only the relevant traces.

nodes.label: Present Representative
nodes.summary: Current executable state of the EG-Desk world.
nodes.body:
# Present Representative

Present is the current executable state.

It includes:

- visible Desk, Agenda, and Card state
- open browser profiles and pages
- active terminal processes
- current files and repo state
- running helper services
- current user intent and selected context
- available actors, tools, permissions, and runtime bindings

Present answers:

```text
What is live right now?
What can be acted on right now?
What changed since the last observed state?
```

The Present Representative is where EG-Desk differs from a passive knowledge base. It binds ontology to executable surfaces.

action projection"] end Rail["Identity Rail
selected concept focus"] Binding["Cross-Facet Binding
identity, sourceRef, causality"] Canonical --> Space Canonical --> Topology Canonical --> Storage Canonical --> Time Canonical --> Intent Canonical --> Action Space --> ChatCard Topology --> Runtime Storage --> SessionFile Time --> MemoryTrace Intent --> ContextBinding Action --> MessageEvents ChatCard -. same identity .-> Rail Runtime -. same identity .-> Rail SessionFile -. same identity .-> Rail MemoryTrace -. same identity .-> Rail ContextBinding -. same identity .-> Rail MessageEvents -. same identity .-> Rail Rail --> Binding Binding -. selected only .-> ChatCard Binding -. selected only .-> Runtime Binding -. selected only .-> SessionFile Binding -. selected only .-> MemoryTrace Binding -. selected only .-> ContextBinding Binding -. selected only .-> MessageEvents ``` ## Reading Rule The diagram should be read as: ```text one identity many facet projections selected-focus binding ``` It should not be read as one global containment tree.

nodes.label: Identity Rail
nodes.summary: UI rail that shows all known projections of the selected canonical concept.
nodes.body:
# Identity Rail

The identity rail is the UI that keeps a selected canonical concept stable across lens changes.

For example:

```text
Selected: entity.llm_chat_session

Space     -> Chat Card on Desk
Topology  -> runtime session using CPU/RAM
Storage   -> session JSONL on Disk
Time      -> Past memory trace
Intent    -> active context/goal binding
Action    -> message-send / file-read / context-assemble
```

The identity rail prevents the user from confusing facet projections with different concepts.

nodes.label: View Projection
nodes.summary: A user-facing assembled view made from one facet or a controlled combination of facets.
nodes.body:
# View Projection

A view projection is the assembled view the user sees.

It can be:

- single-facet view: `Space`, `Topology`, `Time`, `Storage`, `Intent`, `Action`
- controlled cross-facet view: selected object projected across several facets
- curated About/Vision view: a guided read-only explanation

## Renderer Rule

```text
Default:
  one primary facet at a time

On selection:
  keep canonical identity
  show related projections in identity rail
  reveal cross-facet connectors only for selected concept
```

This keeps the canvas readable while preserving multi-facet truth.

nodes.label: Time-Sliced Flat Deck
nodes.summary: Interactive flat-deck visualization method for EG-Desk ontology panes.
nodes.body:
# Time-Sliced Flat Deck

This view renders the EG-Desk ontology as a set of flat 2D pane surfaces seen from a shallow 2.5D camera angle.

The camera angle is only a reading aid. Pane thickness is not semantic. The ontology still uses three primary axes:

```text
Time
Space
Virtual
```

The rendered pane is a coordinate cell where time and physical/virtual depth are applied together:

```text
Rendered Pane = TimeSlice x DepthLayer

TimeSlice  = past | present | future | multiverse
DepthLayer = physical | binding | virtual
```

## Why This View Exists

The ontology cannot be read well as a simple node graph because the same concept can participate in several assemblies:

```text
desktop
  -> terminal
      -> cpu
      -> ram
      -> disk

entity.llm_chat_session
  -> chat card on desktop
  -> runtime through terminal
  -> session file on disk
  -> context binding
  -> future goal
```

The flat-deck view makes those assemblies browsable without duplicating objects across panes.

## Home Pane Rule

Each object has exactly one home pane in this view.

```text
object
  -> one visible home card
  -> optional ghost/reference context elsewhere
```

Do not draw the same object as a full card in multiple panes. For example, `desktop` belongs to the present physical pane. A future goal may reference the desktop, but the future pane should not contain another full `desktop` card.

Default home placement:

```text
past
  -> chat memory
  -> memory trace
  -> evidence/history files

present physical
  -> desktop
  -> terminal
  -> cpu
  -> ram
  -> disk
  -> concrete files/cards/runtime surfaces

present binding
  -> topology use
  -> storage link
  -> action path
  -> context binding

present virtual
  -> entity.llm_chat_session
  -> egdesk.desk
  -> egdesk.agenda
  -> egdesk.card

future
  -> goal
  -> plan
  -> task
  -> structured output

multiverse
  -> alternate plan
  -> candidate future
```

## Visual Grammar

The canvas should show structure with geometry, not explanatory labels.

```text
left/right position  -> time
up/down depth        -> virtual / binding / physical emphasis
large active deck    -> currently selected time slice
dim side deck        -> adjacent time context
node card            -> object's home pane
thin ghost node      -> context/reference only
orthogonal line      -> assembly or relation direction
side panel           -> relation meaning and selected details
```

Canvas labels should name objects, not schema categories. Avoid visible labels such as axis, physical, virtual, binding, topology, storage, intent, or action unless the user is explicitly editing the model.

Do not subdivide the active pane with visible internal rectangles. Physical/virtual depth should be readable from vertical placement, containment paths, connector ports, and the right-side lens state.

## Relation Line Rule

Relation lines on the canvas show only existence, direction, and emphasis.

The relation type, source/target text, and explanation belong in the right-side detail panel.

Preferred line style:

```text
long orthogonal connector
square turns
thin stroke
subtle arrow endpoint
no relation label chip on canvas
```

Assembly examples:

```text
desktop
|_____
|     |
terminal
|_____
|  |  |
cpu ram disk
```

For time-crossing relations, use a horizontal-forward path:

```text
past evidence -> present context -> future goal
```

The time axis is visually left-to-right. It is not bidirectional unless the view is explicitly about rewind, comparison, or branching.

## Interaction Grammar

The view is a lens, not a mode toolbar.

```text
Lens = selected object/relation + active TimeSlice + active DepthLayer
```

Expected interaction:

```text
horizontal trackpad scroll -> move active time slice
vertical trackpad scroll   -> emphasize depth layer
pinch or Cmd/Ctrl + wheel  -> semantic zoom
blank deck drag            -> card-local pan
empty pane click           -> pane inventory
object click               -> object focus
relation stroke click      -> side-panel relation detail
```

Do not expose product-facing buttons named focus, hierarchy, time, spatial, virtual, physical, or tilt. Those are implementation terms.

## Active Pane Behavior

The active pane should be visually dominant.

```text
active pane
  -> high opacity
  -> trapezoid desk surface, with the back edge narrower than the front edge
  -> all home objects for that pane visible
  -> selected and connected objects sharp
  -> unrelated objects dimmed but still locatable

adjacent panes
  -> lower opacity
  -> only home objects or ghost context needed for reading the selected path
```

When an object is selected, connected upper/lower depth objects may become sharper. This should feel like moving the lens through the deck, not switching to a separate graph mode.

## Non-Goals

This view is not:

- a Wikipedia-style concept definition page
- a global force-directed graph
- a generic graph database browser
- a 3D model where pane thickness carries meaning
- a subagent topology diagram

Subagents and tools can be shown as runtime actors inside the ontology, but they are not the foundation of the visualization.

nodes.label: Time-Sliced Spatial Pane
nodes.summary: A physical pane is a surface object; a time-sliced spatial pane is a virtual wrapper assembled from physical panes at a specific time.
nodes.body:
# Time-Sliced Spatial Pane

Separate the physical object from the virtual assembly.

```text
physical pane = visible surface/container object
time-local virtual pane = semantic layer assembled from physical panes in one time slice
trajectory pane = composed virtual space across past/present/future slices
time-sliced spatial pane = virtual pane at time T
```

Objects live on physical panes.

The renderer should also wrap the virtual pane that emerges inside each time slice. Past, present, and future all have this split:

```text
time slice
  physical pane wrapper
  time-local virtual pane wrapper
```

Virtual concepts and entities are overlays or identity bindings attached to objects on the physical panes and to the assembled virtual pane.

## Layout Rule

```text
Past Pane     Present Pane(active)     Future Pane
space@past    space@present            space@future
```

Inside the active pane:

```text
space objects
  -> cards, files, runtime resources, surfaces

binding band
  -> storage, topology, intent, action

virtual overlay
  -> canonical identity, entity meaning, goals, context binding
```

Time arranges pane assemblies. Space fills physical panes. Virtual explains identity and meaning on top of objects and across the assembled pane.

## Rendering Rule

The product view should show three containment levels:

- physical pane wrapper: the actual surface/container that objects occupy
- time-local virtual pane wrapper: the semantic layer assembled inside one time slice
- trajectory pane wrapper: the composed semantic/time-space across past, present, and future

The wrappers can be unlabeled in the main view if position, emphasis, and contained objects make the relation inferable.

Canvas labels should name objects, not schema categories. Terms such as axis, binding, physical, and virtual can guide layout and selection emphasis, but they should not dominate the visible node labels.

## Inventory Rule

A pane can be selected directly.

```text
pane selection
  -> inventory of objects in that time-local pane
  -> object selection
  -> object focus
```

Pane inventory should expose multiple co-present objects without drawing every global edge. It should still draw bounded node-to-node connectors for actual co-present graph edges. Depth bands and rails only explain physical / binding / virtual structure; assembly should use orthogonal tree connectors, for example `desktop -> terminal -> cpu/ram/disk`.

Vertical navigation inside a selected pane should travel depth:

```text
physical
  -> binding
  -> virtual
```

This must be visible through bands, connector ports, and vertical connectors, not through canvas labels alone.
